name: Kuria
confidence_why: Marlo, Mwita and Paster (2015) describe Kuria as a predictable Bantu tone language with toneless verb roots and grammatically assigned H tones, and Philippson (1991), from his own field notes, describes the same system as a culminative accent realised as H tone on the first to fourth mora of the verb stem; the two differ only in whether to call this tone or pitch accent, and neither reports any word stress.
catalog_citation: Marlo, Michael R., Leonard Chacha Mwita & Mary Paster. 2015. Problems in Kuria H tone assignment. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 33(1): 251-265. DOI 10.1007/s11049-014-9251-y (Springer publisher PDF deposited at Kenyatta University IR, handle 123456789/12362)
catalog_locator: Sect. 1 'Mora-counting H tone assignment in Kuria', pp. 251-252 (saved, pp. 1-2)
catalog_quote: Kuria is a ‘predictable’ Bantu tone language (Odden 1989), which lacks lexical tonal contrasts in verb roots: all verb roots are underlyingly toneless (/Ø/). Verbal tone patterns are determined primarily by inflectional H tones that are assigned by rule to different positions of the stem to mark tense-aspect-mood-polarity, focus, and clause-type distinctions—distinctions that are henceforth referred to simply as ‘tense’ distinctions. Most verbal forms in Kuria are inflected with one of four basic tonal patterns that we refer to here as ‘melodies’. These four melodies, illustrated in (1), are characterized by a H tone (the ‘melodic H’) that is assigned to one of the first four moras of the verb stem, depending on the tense (Mwita 2008; Odden 1987). ... Both the surface location of the H and the very presence of the H are determined by the tense category, since at least one tense (namely, the Hortatory Imperative) lacks a melodic H (Mwita 2008:134–135). In tonally inflected tenses, the melodic H spreads rightward from its assigned position onto any and all non-phrase-final moras. Tenses with the µ1 melody, such as the Past, thus have a H tone that begins on the initial mora of the stem and extends rightward to the penult.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kuria (kuri1259) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Philippson's 1991 Paris V thesis (theses.fr: no online copy), was already held by the project from the bemb1257/gwen1239 checks (author's open PDF from the DDL Lyon site) and was copied into the kuri1259 folder and read in full for Kuria. It is relevant: Kuria is in the sample from the author's own field notes and treated at length (pp. 271-273, 413, 462, 464, 477, 485, Annexe p. 502). Philippson's 'accent' for Kuria is a culminative H tone (pitch accent): noun stems have a single prosodic scheme with the H normally on the initial stem mora and no lexical contrast; verb forms take the H on the 1st-4th mora of the maximal stem by tense, with tone doubling (blocked from penult onto final). Kuria keeps a vowel-length contrast and is not among the languages he lists with penultimate length or pitch culmination; the thesis contains no statement of intensity/length word stress for Kuria. direct downloads found the Persée landing page of Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2014 'Kuria tone melodies' (Africana Linguistica 20: 277-294; PDF altcha-blocked; a verb-tone study, not a stress source) and no open copy of Odden 1987 (OSU page 404). The prior records Cammenga 1994 (thesis) and 2004 (Köppe grammar, Harvard print) and Aksenova & Toporova 1994 as print-only; Cammenga 2004 remains the likely best place for an explicit Kuria stress/penult statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No opened source says anything about word stress in Kuria. The word prosody is a grammatically predictable two-tone (H vs toneless/L) system: verb roots have no lexical tone; each tense assigns one 'melodic' H to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th mora of the (macro)stem, and that H spreads rightward to the penultimate mora (never onto the phrase-final syllable); nouns carry an H normally on the first mora of the root (Diercks et al. 2015 fn 1; Philippson 1991 p. 502). Philippson 1991 (pp. 271-273, 502) reanalyses the same facts as a 'langue à accent' whose accents are realised as H tones (a pitch accent reading), with the accent on one of the first four moras of the maximal verb stem and normally on the stem-initial mora in nominals; he explicitly lists no intensity/length culmination for Kuria.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by any source (the H-tone spreading to the penult is not described as stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Hortatory Imperative has no melodic H (Marlo et al. 2015: 252, citing Mwita 2008: 134-135); some constructions carry both a µ1 and a µ4 H; NonFinality blocks spreading into the phrase-final syllable, whose vowel is lengthened; spreading differs in the Nyabaasi dialect (fn 3, citing Odden 1987 and Cammenga 2004); speakers differ in phrasal H assignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Verb (macro)stem in phrasal context; the H-assignment/spreading is described as a phrase-level process referring to the internal structure of the verbal word (Buguumbe dialect, Kuria District, Kenya). Noun tone from citation forms in isolation (Mwita 2012). No statement about stress at either word or phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2015 describe the Buguumbe dialect of Kuria (Kuria District, SW Kenya; data mainly from co-author Mwita, a native speaker); Odden 1987 and Cammenga 2004 concern the Nyabaasi dialect, where H spreading differs (fn 3). Philippson 1991 treats 'kuria' (E43) from his own field notes plus Odden and Whiteley. All are the language-level kuri1259 (no separate dialect glottocodes cited).

new_statements.quote: Il s'agit d'une langue à accent [fn. 1: Les accents sont réalisés comme des tons H.] dont les équivalents-radicaux n'ont pas de propriété prosodique distinctive En d'autres termes, tous les verbes ont le même profil mélodique à un tiroir donné. L'accent dans les formes verbales peut se placer sur une des quatre premières mores du thème maximal (noter qu'une règle de répétition tonale assez classique associe le H également à la more suivant la more accentuée)
new_statements.translation: It is an accent language [fn. 1: the accents are realised as H tones] whose root-equivalents have no distinctive prosodic property; in other words, all verbs have the same melodic profile in a given tense. The accent in verb forms can be placed on one of the first four moras of the maximal stem (note that a fairly classic tone-doubling rule links the H also to the mora following the accented mora).

new_statements.reading: First-hand (author's own field notes, Sources p. 515, plus Odden 1987 and Whiteley 1955). Kuria is described as a pitch accent (culminative H-tone) language: no lexical prosodic contrast in noun stems (one scheme, H normally on the initial mora of the stem) or in verb roots; in verbs the H is placed by tense on the 1st-4th mora of the maximal stem, with doubling onto the next mora except from penult onto final. This is tone/pitch accent placement, not intensity or length stress; Philippson does not list Kuria among languages with penultimate length or pitch culmination (p. 484) and gives no statement of demarcative word stress. For a stress catalog, Kuria would be recorded as 'no stress statement; tonal (grammatical pitch accent) system' on this source, pending Cammenga 1994/2004 (print only).

new_statements.quote: [p. 102] In Kuria there are two level contrastive tones; high and low, to which may be added a rising tone from low to high,and a falling tone from high to low. [...] [p. 103] While significant semantic tone is rare, - I have no examples in radicals - ,the significance of grammatical tone is considerable, even for the purely practical student of the language. [...] As might be expected in a language where pitch is significant,stress is characteristic rather than distinctive. In verbals there is a stress on the radical,and on V(owel)1 and V(owel)3 in poly-syllabic radicals: in radicals of shape -C- a stress occurs on the syllable immediately preceding the radical.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification tonal, no stress rule, from Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2015: Kuria a 'predictable' tone language with toneless verb roots) and with Philippson 1991 (culminative H / accent tonal system, no lexical prosodic contrast in verb roots): Whiteley likewise finds two contrastive tones, grammatical rather than lexical tone and no tonal contrasts in radicals. It ADDS the first explicit stress statement held by the project: stress exists but is non-contrastive and sits on the verb radical (root-initial vowel, plus V3 of long radicals; pre-radical syllable for -C- roots). Nothing in the catalog is contradicted; the catalog's empty 'rule' could be annotated '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kuria (Butimbaru dialect, Tarime) has two contrastive level tones (H, L; plus rising and falling), with tone mostly grammatical rather than lexical (no tonal contrasts found in verb radicals). Stress is non-distinctive ('characteristic rather than distinctive'): in verbals a stress falls on the radical, i.e. on the first vowel of the verb root, and in polysyllabic radicals on the first and third vowels of the radical; with vowel-less radicals of shape -C- the stress falls on the syllable immediately preceding the radical. This is a morphologically anchored (root-initial), non-phonemic stress in a tone language; the statement covers verbals only (the thesis is about the verbal) and says nothing about stress in nouns or about penultimate prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not labelled as such, but 'on V(owel)1 and V(owel)3 in poly-syllabic radicals' describes a second stress on the third vowel of long radicals, i.e. an alternating (every other vowel) rhythm counted from the root-initial vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Radicals of shape -C- (no vowel): stress shifts to the syllable immediately preceding the radical. No other exceptions; no statement for non-verbal words.
new_statements.identity_note: Whiteley describes the Butimbaru (Timbaru) dialect of Kuria as spoken at Tarime, North Mara, Tanganyika, recorded 1953-Feb. 1955 ('All my main informants used the Butimbaru dialect, and it is this form as it was being spoken in Tarime during the past two years that I have attempted to record', Introduction, p. ~9); the catalog sources (Marlo et al. 2015; Mwita) describe Kenyan Kuria (Nyabaasi etc.), Philippson 1991 his own Kuria field notes plus Whiteley and Odden.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement. Within the existing statements there is a framing difference, not a placement conflict: Marlo, Mwita & Paster (2015) treat Kuria as a predictable Bantu tone language with toneless verb roots and grammatically assigned H tones and say nothing about stress, while Philippson (1991) calls it a 'langue à accent' whose accents are realised as H tones (culminative grammatical H, normally on the initial mora of noun stems, tense-determined position in verbs). Both agree there is no lexical prosodic contrast and neither gives a demarcative word-stress rule; Philippson's 'accent' is pitch, not intensity/length stress. The catalog record for Kuria has an empty rule and is best left as tonal / no stress statement.
